reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: The severe end of the collagen VI-related spectrum, of which Bethlem myopathy is the milder counterpart, usually presenting at birth or in early infancy
Neonates show marked hypotonia and weakness together with the striking combination of proximal joint contractures (hips, knees, elbows) and hyperlaxity of the distal joints (wrists, fingers, ankles)
Congenital features may include torticollis, kyphoscoliosis, hip dislocation and prominent calcanei
Motor milestones are delayed and many children achieve, but may later lose, independent walking
Caused by mutations in the collagen VI genes COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3, with both recessive and dominant (often de novo) inheritance recognised
Progressive respiratory failure from diaphragmatic and chest-wall weakness is a leading concern and often necessitates non-invasive nocturnal ventilatory support
Soft, velvety palms and follicular hyperkeratosis with abnormal scarring reflect the underlying connective-tissue defect
reference.pathophysiology: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the collagen VI genes COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3, which more severely disrupt the assembly or function of the collagen VI microfibrillar network than the milder variants causing Bethlem myopathy. Collagen VI links the muscle-fibre basement membrane to the surrounding interstitial matrix, and its severe deficiency impairs the structural and signalling relationship between fibres and their environment, with dysregulated mitochondrial function and increased apoptosis contributing to early and profound muscle degeneration. Because collagen VI is widespread in connective tissue, the disorder also produces the characteristic joint contractures and hyperlaxity, skeletal deformity and skin abnormalities, and the early respiratory failure that dominates its natural history.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital muscular dystrophies including merosin-deficient forms
Congenital myopathies such as core and nemaline myopathies
Distal arthrogryposis and syndromic contracture disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, usually normal or only mildly elevated
Muscle biopsy with collagen VI immunohistochemistry, often supplemented by fibroblast culture studies
Targeted genetic testing of COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3
Muscle magnetic resonance imaging showing the characteristic pattern of muscle involvement
Respiratory function tests and overnight monitoring for hypoventilation from early in the disease
Spinal and hip imaging to assess scoliosis and dislocation
redFlags: Progressive respiratory failure or nocturnal hypoventilation, which may occur even before loss of walking
Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising respiratory function
Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive in infancy
Loss of ambulation requiring orthopaedic and rehabilitation planning
reference.prognosis: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy is more severe than Bethlem myopathy, with many affected children losing ambulation in the first or second decade and developing progressive respiratory insufficiency that determines survival, although proactive respiratory and orthopaedic care can substantially prolong and improve life.
pitfalls: Delaying respiratory surveillance because motor function seems relatively preserved
Overlooking the diagnostic combination of proximal contractures with distal hyperlaxity in a hypotonic infant
Assuming normal collagen VI immunostaining excludes the diagnosis, as staining can be only partially reduced
Not recognising that dominant de novo mutations can cause the disorder in a child with no family history
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-specific drug therapy exists for this collagen VI deficiency, so care is anticipatory and supportive around respiratory, orthopaedic and functional needs
Proactive respiratory management with non-invasive nocturnal ventilation for hypoventilation and airway-clearance techniques, given progressive diaphragmatic and chest-wall weakness
Physiotherapy with stretching, serial casting and orthoses to manage proximal contractures while preserving distal hyperlaxity
Orthopaedic surveillance and intervention for kyphoscoliosis and hip dislocation
Regular monitoring of respiratory function and overnight oximetry from early in the disease, with nutritional and feeding support
Multidisciplinary care through neuromuscular, respiratory, orthopaedic, physiotherapy and occupational therapy teams to maintain ambulation as long as possible
Genetic counselling given COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3 mutations with both dominant and recessive inheritance
